newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-UEFA AND ENGLAND CALL WORLD CUP TRUCE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-UEFA AND ENGLAND CALL WORLD CUP TRUCE.

text.p: UEFA reached a truce with the English Football Association (F.A.) on Friday in the row over the 2006 World Cup finals by withdrawing its unequivocal support for Germany's bid.
European soccer's governing body agreed to meet officials from both England and Germany at a meeting in Geneva in April.
The officials will present their ideas on how Europe can whittle down its World Cup candidates wanting to host the finals to just one country.
If all sides can agree on how such a process would work, England, Germany and any other interested European country will then present their bids to UEFA.
UEFA will decide in December 1998 which bid to submit to FIFA, who will announce the venue in June 2000.
The latest UEFA proposal, disclosed at a joint news conference with the F.A. in London after three hours of negotiations, represents a significant change of heart on UEFA's part.
Just last week they sent a fax to the F.A. saying they were openly backing Germany's World Cup bid, which has been on the table since June 1993.
The F.A. were outraged. UEFA responded by claiming their position had been clear for over two years and the F.A. knew full well of their support for Germany.
On Friday UEFA denied they had been forced to climb down in the row, saying the situation had changed since last week and they had reviewed their position accordingly.
"Until a week ago there was only bid...UEFA had agreed to put forward one bid. Now we have two bids and we have to decide," UEFA general secretary Gerhard Aigner told reporters.
"UEFA is doing its utmost to have a harmonious bidding process within its federation."
He said UEFA was anxious to prevent a repeat of the bitter wrangling which marred the bidding process for the 2002 World Cup, eventually awarded jointly to regional rivals South Korea and Japan.
"What we want to avoid is a heavy race going on right up until the FIFA deadline (in February 1999)," he said.
"There should be no excessive competition between countries bidding for such an event. The April meeting is about creating a machinery and a process by which we can proceed."
The F.A. said it was delighted with the outcome of what it described as "very worthwhile talks".
"All the F.A. have ever sought is a proper and reasonable way in which England can make a bid for the 2006 World Cup," the association's chief executive Graham Kelly said.
"In the end we hope there will be rules laid down in Geneva which will apply for World Cup bidding in the future."
F.A. chairman Keith Wiseman said the English had not compromised their position in Friday's meeting.
"I don't think we have had to move at all...no admissions of any kind have been made by anybody."
And the German F.A., which had counted on UEFA's backing, also seemed happy with the deal.

"I think it is completely fair from UEFA's point of view that England's arguments are heard," German Soccer Association (DFB) spokesman Wolfgang Niersbach said. "But the DFB is unchanged in its view that UEFA will support our bid."
"We're staying calm and collected," he said.
